answer.summary: Eyal says procrastination is usually an emotion-regulation problem: people avoid a task to escape discomfort, not because they are broken. He recommends noticing and naming the feeling, then using tools such as the 10-minute rule to stay with the urge and return to the task. [S1, S2, S3, S4]

sections.heading: Why people procrastinate
sections.content: Eyal describes procrastination as an emotion-regulation problem, not a character flaw. A difficult or unpleasant task can bring up feelings such as boredom, anxiety, stress, loneliness, or frustration; people procrastinate or distract themselves to escape those feelings. He argues the issue is not necessarily technology: even without apps, he found himself inventing other distractions. [S1, S2, S4]

sections.heading: What to do when discomfort prompts distraction
sections.content: First, identify the internal trigger—the feeling or “itch” you want to escape—and recognize it as a feeling rather than evidence that something is wrong with you. Instead of immediately escaping it, Eyal recommends using the discomfort to move toward the task. One concrete tool is the 10-minute rule: take a deep breath, repeat a personal mantra (his is, “This is what it feels like to get better”), and keep at the task until the feeling crests and subsides. He says that often, by the end of the 10 minutes, the urge has passed and you can resume working; over time, you can extend the interval to 12 or 20 minutes. He also names surfing the urge and reimagining the task as other techniques. [S2, S3, S4, S10]
